body:
Understanding the landscapes of Kutch

Kutch, also written as Kachchh, is situated in western Gujarat. Its cultural landscape includes arid agricultural land, saline marshes, grasslands, coastal settlements and traditional craft-producing villages.

Low and irregular rainfall, high evaporation and widespread salinity influence the region's livelihoods. Agriculture, pastoralism, salt production, fishing, trade and handicrafts have developed in response to different local conditions.

The Great Rann and the Little Rann

The Rann of Kutch consists of extensive low-lying saline landscapes. Seasonal inundation and subsequent evaporation create marked differences between the monsoon and dry seasons.

LandscapePrincipal characteristicsCultural or livelihood association
Great Rann of KutchExtensive seasonal saline marshWhite salt landscape and Rann Utsav near Dhordo
Little Rann of KutchSeasonally inundated saline landAgariya salt workers and Indian wild ass habitat
Banni grasslandsGrassland ecosystem adjoining the Great RannMaldhari pastoralism and livestock-based livelihoods

During the monsoon, parts of the Rann become inundated. As water evaporates during the dry season, salts remain on the surface, producing the characteristic white landscape.

Agariya salt workers

The Agariyas are traditionally associated with salt production, particularly in the Little Rann of Kutch. Salt production involves bringing saline water or brine into shallow salt pans, where solar evaporation concentrates the dissolved salts and causes salt crystals to form.

This occupation is seasonal because salt production requires suitable dry conditions. Monsoon inundation interrupts production. Salt workers therefore depend closely on the seasonal behaviour of the landscape.

Banni and the Maldhari tradition

Banni is a grassland region situated along the southern margin of the Great Rann. Its traditional economy is closely connected with livestock rearing and grazing.

Maldhari is a broad occupational and cultural term for traditional livestock-keeping communities. It does not denote a single caste or tribe. Rabaris, Jats and other pastoral communities contribute to the wider pastoral culture of Kutch.

Pastoral households rear animals such as cattle, buffaloes, sheep, goats and camels according to their local circumstances. Banni is particularly associated with buffalo rearing and dairy-based livelihoods. Animal husbandry also supports crafts using wool, leather and livestock accessories.

The seasonal availability of fodder and water may require livestock keepers to move their animals between grazing areas. However, not every pastoral household follows a nomadic lifestyle.

Virda: traditional freshwater harvesting

Salinity makes access to drinking water an important challenge in Banni. A virda is a traditional shallow well that enables communities to obtain relatively fresh rainwater stored beneath the surface in otherwise saline surroundings.

Such wells are commonly associated with seasonal water catchment areas. Traditional knowledge of local soils, rainfall and water movement helps pastoral communities identify suitable locations.

Bhunga settlements

The bhunga is a traditional circular dwelling characteristic of Kutch. It commonly has thick earthen walls and a conical roof constructed using locally available materials.

Earthen walls help moderate indoor temperatures. The compact circular form and relatively lightweight roof are also associated with resilience under certain environmental and earthquake conditions, although no traditional structure is completely immune to damage.

Bhunga interiors and walls may be decorated with mud relief and mirror work. The dwelling therefore demonstrates the connection between local building materials, environmental adaptation and artistic tradition.

Rann Utsav

Rann Utsav is a cultural tourism festival associated with the white salt landscape of the Great Rann near Dhordo. It is organised during the dry-season tourism period and showcases regional food, textiles, handicrafts and cultural traditions.

It should be distinguished from traditional tribal and religious fairs. Rann Utsav is a modern organised tourism festival that provides a platform for older Kutchi cultural traditions.

Prelims focus

  • Agariyas are traditionally associated with salt production.
  • Banni is a grassland and pastoral landscape.
  • Maldhari is a broad term for livestock-keeping communities.
  • Virda is a traditional freshwater harvesting well.
  • Bhunga is a characteristic circular dwelling of Kutch.
  • Trap: Dhordo and Rann Utsav are associated with the Great Rann, whereas the Little Rann is particularly associated with salt production and the Indian wild ass.

[References: Gujarat Tourism, Great Rann of Kutch and Rann Utsav; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, Kutch and Wild Ass Sanctuary; G.B. Pant National Institute of Himalayan Environment, Compendium on Indian Biosphere Reserves: Progression During Two Decades of Conservation, chapter 16, Kachchh, p. 164; Climate Change Adaptation for Natural Resource Dependent Communities in Kachchh, Gujarat, project report, p. 26; Central Arid Zone Research Institute, Desert Environment Newsletter, volume 24, issues 3-4, section on traditional water harvesting in Banni. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

title: Kutch: Salt Marshes, Pastoral Grasslands and Traditional Settlements

body:
Crafts as expressions of regional identity

The handicrafts of Kutch and Saurashtra reflect community traditions, locally available materials, historical trade connections and the needs of agricultural and pastoral households.

Crafts are used in clothing, weddings, festivals, domestic decoration and livestock management. The same skills also support commercial livelihoods when artisans produce textiles and decorative objects for wider markets.

Distinguishing major textile traditions

Bandhani

Bandhani, also called Bandhej, is a traditional resist-dyeing technique. Small portions of fabric are tightly tied before dyeing so that the tied areas resist the dye. Removing the ties reveals characteristic dotted patterns.

Jamnagar, Bhuj and Mandvi are important centres associated with Bandhani. The technique is used to produce saris, odhnis, turbans and bridal textiles.

Patola

Patan in North Gujarat is famous for its traditional double ikat Patola, particularly associated with the Salvi weaving tradition.

In ikat, yarns are resist-dyed before weaving. The warp consists of the lengthwise threads of the fabric, while the weft consists of the crosswise threads. In double ikat, both sets of threads are patterned before weaving and carefully aligned to produce the intended design.

Rajkot is also associated with Patola weaving, particularly single ikat traditions, in which only one set of yarns is resist-dyed before weaving.

Ajrakh

Ajrakh is a traditional resist block-printed textile associated with Kutch and the Khatri artisan tradition. Dhamadka and Ajrakhpur are important centres.

Geometrical patterns, repeated motifs and combinations of indigo, red and other colours are characteristic of traditional Ajrakh textiles. The craft has historical connections with the wider Sindh region.

Kutchi embroidery

Embroidery involves decorating an existing fabric through needlework. Kutch is particularly known for colourful embroidery, mirror work and community-specific designs.

The term Banni embroidery broadly refers to embroidery traditions associated with the Banni region. It is not the name of a single community or one uniform embroidery stitch.

TraditionIdentifying association
Rabari embroideryPastoral community identity, bold decorative patterns and mirror work
Jat embroideryCommunity-specific patterns, including intricate geometrical designs
Mutava embroideryFine geometrical embroidery associated with the Banni region
Ahir embroideryCommunity-specific embroidery with colourful decorative motifs
Soof embroideryCounted-thread geometrical needlework
Bavaliya or HurmitchA traditional interlacing embroidery stitch

Embroidery may decorate garments, wall hangings, bags, cushion covers and wedding textiles. A toran is a decorative hanging used above a doorway, while a chakla is traditionally a square decorative textile.

Other important craft centres

PlaceCraftIdentifying feature
Bhujodi, KutchHandloom weavingShawls, blankets and other woven textiles
Nirona, KutchRogan paintingOil-based decorative painting on cloth
Nirona, KutchBell-making and lacquer workTraditional metal and wooden craft objects
Khavda, KutchPotteryDecorated earthenware
Banni villages, KutchLippan or mud-and-mirror workDecorative earthen relief with mirrors
Jamnagar, SaurashtraBandhaniTie-resist-dyed fabric
Surat, South GujaratZariDecorative metallic thread

Rogan painting

Rogan painting is a particularly distinctive craft associated with Nirona. The word Rogan refers to an oil-based preparation. A thick colour paste, traditionally prepared using oil such as castor oil and pigments, is used to create designs on fabric.

The Tree of Life is a well-known motif associated with Rogan painting. Rogan is a painting tradition and must not be confused with Bandhani dyeing, Ajrakh block printing or Patola weaving.

Crafts and pastoral livelihoods

Woollen shawls, livestock bells, leather products, embroidered garments and animal accessories demonstrate the close relationship between traditional occupations and handicrafts. Pastoral communities historically created or purchased these objects for practical and ceremonial use, while artisan communities developed specialised skills to produce them.

Prelims focus

  • Patan Patola is particularly associated with double ikat and Salvi weavers.
  • Bandhani is tie-resist dyeing, while Ajrakh is resist block printing.
  • Bhujodi is associated with handloom weaving.
  • Nirona is associated with Rogan painting and the Tree of Life motif.
  • Bavaliya is an embroidery stitch, whereas Banni is a geographical region.
  • Trap: Patola patterns are created through pre-dyed yarns and weaving, not through embroidery on finished cloth.

[References: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Crafts Heritage, pp. 9-12; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, Cultural Heritage of India: Traditional Handicraft and Fine Arts, pp. 9-10; District Kachchh, Government of Gujarat, Handicraft; Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, Mapping Indian Textiles, Gujarat and Kutch embroidery sections; Cooper Hewitt Smithsonian Design Museum, Dress, accession 1966-9-1; Garvi Gurjari, Double Ikat Patola textile description; Government of Gujarat, Craft of Gujarat, One District One Product list, Patan and Rajkot weaving entries; Gujarat Tourism, Nirona and Mud Work; Ministry of Tourism, Incredible India, Crafts of Kutch. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

title: Regional Textile Traditions and Handicrafts of Kutch and Saurashtra

body:
The coastal cultural landscape

Saurashtra is a peninsula situated between the Gulf of Kutch and the Gulf of Khambhat, with the Arabian Sea along its western and southern sides. Its coastal settlements have historically developed livelihoods based on fishing, maritime trade, navigation and related occupations.

The availability of marine resources encourages fishing, while access to the sea facilitates trade and cultural exchange. Coastal Gujarat also contains important religious centres, where pilgrimage supports local commerce and hospitality.

Fishing and associated occupations

Veraval, Mangrol and Porbandar are important fishing centres on the Saurashtra coast. Traditional fishing communities include groups such as Kharvas and Kolis, although fishing is not restricted to these communities.

Fishing supports several interconnected activities. These include the construction and repair of boats, preparation and maintenance of nets, landing and sorting fish, preservation, processing and sale.

Traditionally, drying and salting helped preserve fish where refrigeration was unavailable. Modern fishing activities also make use of ice, cold storage, motorised vessels and processing facilities.

Fish-based dishes form part of the food culture of several coastal communities. This illustrates the variation within Gujarat's wider culinary heritage, which also contains extensive vegetarian traditions.

Mandvi and wooden shipbuilding

Mandvi in Kutch is an important example of Gujarat's traditional maritime culture. It developed as a port near the meeting point of the Rukmavati River and the Gulf of Kutch.

The town is associated with wooden shipbuilding and the maritime skills of Kharva communities. Its historical importance reflects Gujarat's commercial connections with other regions across the Arabian Sea.

Mandvi demonstrates that maritime culture is not confined to Saurashtra. Kutch also contains significant coastal and seafaring traditions.

Coastal pilgrimage and regional fairs

Several pilgrimage centres connect Gujarat's coastal geography with religious traditions. Other important regional fairs take place inland but contribute to the broader cultural identity of Saurashtra.

Place or fairLocationPrincipal association
DwarkaDevbhumi DwarkaKrishna worship and Janmashtami
SomnathPrabhas Patan, Gir SomnathShiva worship and Jyotirlinga pilgrimage
Madhavpur FairMadhavpur Ghed, PorbandarMarriage tradition of Krishna and Rukmini
Bhavnath FairFoot of Girnar, JunagadhMaha Shivaratri
Tarnetar FairSurendranagarTrinetreshwar Mahadev Temple and embroidered umbrellas

Madhavpur Fair

Madhavpur Fair is held at Madhavpur Ghed in Porbandar district around Ram Navami in the month of Chaitra. According to religious tradition, it commemorates the marriage of Krishna and Rukmini.

The fair also has a cultural connection with Arunachal Pradesh through traditions concerning Rukmini and the Mishmi community. Celebrations bring together cultural traditions from western and northeastern India.

Tarnetar Fair

Tarnetar Fair takes place near the Trinetreshwar Mahadev Temple in Surendranagar district, traditionally during the month of Bhadrapad. Its cultural associations include elaborately embroidered umbrellas and traditional community gatherings, particularly among Koli participants.

The fair is also associated with a local tradition concerning Draupadi's swayamvara from the Mahabharata. This association is a religious and cultural legend rather than an independently established historical event.

Prelims focus

  • Veraval, Mangrol and Porbandar are important Saurashtra fishing centres.
  • Mandvi in Kutch is associated with wooden shipbuilding.
  • Madhavpur Fair commemorates the Krishna-Rukmini marriage tradition.
  • Madhavpur Fair has a cultural connection with Arunachal Pradesh.
  • Tarnetar Fair is associated with Trinetreshwar Mahadev Temple and embroidered umbrellas.
  • Trap: Tarnetar and Bhavnath are important Saurashtra fairs but are not coastal fishing festivals.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, Heritage of India, pp. 3-4; Gujarat Tourism, Mandvi Beach, Madhavpur Fair, Tarnetar Fair and Bhavnath Fair; Directorate of Economics and Statistics, Evaluation and Assessment of Economic Losses for Fisheries Sector in Gujarat, sections 2.7-2.8; Marine Products Export Development Authority, Major Fishing Harbors, Gujarat entries; NCERT, India: Unity in Cultural Diversity, Gujarat, pp. 35-37. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]
